title: Discharge, transfers and carers
blurb: Plan safe discharge and transfer using discharge to assess pathways 0–3, NICE NG27 and the duties to involve and assess carers.
question: Mrs Ward, 86, is medically fit after a hip fracture but not yet walking safely. Her son asks for her to go straight from the ward into a permanent nursing home. What does current discharge guidance recommend?

teach.h: Safe discharge is planned from admission
teach.body: Discharge is a transition of care, not an event at the end of a stay. NICE NG27 says assessment of health and social care needs and discharge planning should start as soon as people with complex needs are admitted. In England, discharge to assess (D2A) means giving short-term care, rehabilitation and reablement where needed, then assessing longer-term needs once the person has reached optimal recovery, at home or in a step-down bed. In plain English: get people home or to recovery quickly, then decide the long term.
teach.cite: NICE NG27 (2015) rec 1.3.9; DHSC Hospital discharge and community support guidance (Jan 2024)

head: Pathway
Where to
Support

New or additional health or social care, e.g. reablement

teach.caption: Hospital discharge and community support guidance (DHSC/NHS England, updated 26 January 2024), Annex B.

teach.body: Waiting in hospital raises the risk of infection, falls and loss of physical and cognitive function. Assessing long-term needs after recovery gives a truer picture. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without first having an opportunity to recover. NICE NG27 adds: people should not have to make decisions about long-term residential or nursing care while in crisis, and pressure for beds must not lead to unplanned, uncoordinated discharges.
teach.cite: Hospital discharge guidance (2024); NICE NG27 recs 1.5.11–1.5.12

teach.caption: NG27 1.5.31: if the plan relies on family or carers, consider their willingness, ability, circumstances and need for respite.

teach.h: Information that must travel with the person
teach.body: Give people information about their diagnoses and treatment and a complete list of their medicines when they move between hospital and home or care home, and to carers if appropriate (NG27 1.1.5). Offer it in accessible formats. Consider giving people with complex needs a contact for medicine or equipment problems in the first 24 hours (1.5.9). If someone is homeless, the discharge coordinator liaises with the local authority housing options team (1.5.28).

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Ward on an orthogeriatric ward
teach.body: Mrs Ward, 86, is medically fit after hip surgery but not yet walking safely. Her son wants a permanent nursing home now. Nurse Leila, the named discharge coordinator, explains discharge to assess: Mrs Ward can go to a community rehabilitation bed (pathway 2) and her long-term needs will be assessed once she has recovered. Leila involves Mrs Ward and her son, sends the medicines list and plan with her, and makes sure the GP gets the summary within 24 hours.

teach.text: Pathway 3 (new care home placement) is for exceptional circumstances. Long-term care decisions are made after recovery, not in hospital and not while the person is in crisis.

items: Discharge planning starts at admission, with a named discharge coordinator.
Pathways: 0 home, no new needs; 1 home with new support; 2 community recovery bed; 3 new care home (exceptional).
D2A: assess long-term needs after recovery; avoid decisions in crisis or rushed discharges for beds.
Involve patients and unpaid carers, including young carers (Care Act s74); tell carers of their right to an assessment (s10).
Send medicines list and plan with the person; summary to GP within 24 hours; follow up those at risk in 24–72 hours.

summary: You can now plan safe discharge and transfer using the discharge to assess pathways and NICE NG27, coordinate information, medicines and equipment across settings, and involve and support carers. You can also evaluate people's experience of transitions.

A.q: Mr Okoro is going home from hospital with a short reablement package that he did not have before admission. Which discharge pathway is this?
options: Pathway 0
Pathway 1
Pathway 2
Pathway 3
A.why: Pathway 1 is discharge home or to a usual place of residence with new or additional health and/or social care needs, such as reablement (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024).

whyNot.0: Pathway 0 is for people with no new or additional care needs.
whyNot.2: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based recovery setting.
whyNot.3: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement.

A.q: According to NICE NG27, by when should a person's discharge summary be available to their GP?
options: Within 72 hours of discharge
Within 7 days of discharge
At the first GP appointment
Within 24 hours of discharge
A.why: NG27 rec 1.5.6: the hospital doctor responsible should ensure the discharge summary is available to the GP within 24 hours of discharge, and a copy given to the person on the day.

whyNot.0: 72 hours is longer than NG27 allows.
whyNot.1: Seven days would leave the GP without key information.
whyNot.2: The GP needs the summary promptly, not at a future appointment.

A.q: Which statement describes the duty on NHS trusts under section 74 of the Care Act 2014, as amended in 2022?
options: Involve patients and unpaid carers in discharge planning
Assess every carer's eligibility for carer's benefits
Provide carers with paid respite care after the discharge
Ask carers to sign the discharge plan
A.why: The Health and Care Act 2022 amended Care Act s74 so NHS trusts must involve patients and unpaid carers (including young carers) as soon as feasible in discharge planning for adults likely to need care and support (Hospital discharge guidance, 2024).

whyNot.1: Benefits assessment is not part of this duty.
whyNot.2: The duty is to involve carers, not to fund respite.
whyNot.3: Carers' signatures are not required; their involvement is.

B.q: Mrs Ward, 86, is medically fit after a hip fracture but not yet walking safely. Her son asks for a permanent nursing home placement directly from the ward. What does current guidance recommend?
options: Discharge her to recover first, then assess long-term needs
Arrange the permanent placement as he requests
Keep her in hospital until her long-term needs are assessed
Discharge her home with no support, as she is medically fit
B.why: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home for the first time without an opportunity to recover (Hospital discharge guidance, 2024; NG27 1.5.11).

whyNot.1: A first permanent placement straight from hospital is for exceptional circumstances only.
whyNot.2: Waiting in hospital raises risks of infection and deconditioning; assessment should follow recovery.
whyNot.3: She has new needs and cannot yet walk safely; discharge needs support.

B.q: What is the role of the discharge coordinator described in NICE NG27?
options: To arrange transport on the day of discharge
To be the central contact for discharge planning
To decide whether the person is medically fit to leave
To approve funding for care packages
B.why: NG27 recs 1.5.1–1.5.2: make a single practitioner responsible for coordinating discharge, acting as the central point of contact for professionals, the person and family, and involved in all discharge decisions.

whyNot.0: Transport may be part of planning, but the role is far wider.
whyNot.2: Medical fitness is a clinical decision by the treating team.
whyNot.3: Funding decisions are made by commissioners and local authorities.

B.q: Sue will care for her husband after his stroke, a new role for her. What should the nurse tell her about support?
options: Carers are assessed when their GP refers them
She must pay a fee to the council for any carer's assessment
She can have a carer's assessment by the council
Carers' needs are assessed at 6 months
B.why: Under Care Act 2014 s10, a local authority must assess a carer who appears to have needs for support. Guidance says no carers should be left without adequate support or a carer's assessment if needed.

whyNot.0: Assessment is a local authority duty and does not depend on asking the GP.
whyNot.1: There is no charge for a carer's assessment.
whyNot.3: The 6-month review relates to carers' training in NG27, not the right to an assessment.

C.q: Kofi, 52, is ready for discharge after pneumonia but has been sleeping rough. What should the discharge coordinator do?
options: Discharge him with a list of night shelters
Keep him in hospital until he finds a tenancy
Ask him to contact housing services himself after discharge
Liaise with the council's housing options team
C.why: NG27 rec 1.5.28: if a person is homeless, the discharge coordinator should liaise with the local authority housing options team so that they are offered advice and help.

whyNot.0: A list alone does not provide coordinated support.
whyNot.1: Keeping a medically fit person in hospital is not the solution and increases risk.
whyNot.2: Leaving it to him after discharge risks him returning to the street unwell.

C.q: Mr Hassan, 79, has heart failure and has been admitted three times this year. He is going home today. What follow-up does NICE NG27 recommend?
options: A routine GP review at the practice in 6 weeks
An outpatient clinic appointment in about 3 months' time
A GP or community nurse call or visit in 24–72 hours
Follow-up arranged if he contacts his GP himself
C.why: NG27 rec 1.5.38: a GP or community-based nurse should phone or visit people at risk of readmission 24–72 hours after discharge.

whyNot.0: Six weeks is too late for someone at high risk of readmission.
whyNot.1: Three months leaves the high-risk early period uncovered.
whyNot.3: Relying on him to call misses early deterioration.

C.q: At 20:00, the bed manager asks a nurse to discharge Mrs Lee home tonight, but the hoist and commode she needs will not arrive until tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain discharge must wait until the equipment is in place
Discharge her, as her family can manage tonight
Discharge her to a chair in the discharge lounge overnight
Discharge her and ask the district nurse to visit next week
C.why: NG27: ensure essential specialist equipment and support is in place at the point of discharge (1.5.18) and pressure to free beds must not lead to unplanned, uncoordinated discharges (1.5.12). The nurse should explain and escalate if needed.

whyNot.1: Without a hoist and commode, safe moving and toileting cannot be assured.
whyNot.2: An overnight lounge stay is unsafe and undignified.
whyNot.3: A visit next week leaves her without essential equipment now.

reteach.title: Packing for the journey
reteach.question: Before a long journey, what do you need to sort out before you leave the house?

blocks.h: The person travels with their plan
blocks.body: Discharge is a journey from one team to another. The person needs a route (the pathway), a guide (the discharge coordinator), luggage (medicines list, plan, equipment) and someone waiting at the other end (GP summary within 24 hours, follow-up for those at risk). Carers are fellow travellers: involve them, and tell them about their right to their own assessment.

blocks.text: 'Medically fit' is not the same as 'safe to go': equipment, support and information must be in place first.

explain.body: 0: home, no new needs. 1: home with new or additional support. 2: community bed with recovery support. 3: new residential or nursing home, exceptional circumstances.

test.q: A woman needs a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed before she can go home. Which pathway is this?
options: Pathway 0
Pathway 1
Pathway 2
Pathway 3
test.why: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, such as a community hospital or rehabilitation bed (Hospital discharge guidance, 2024).

whyNot.0: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.
whyNot.1: Pathway 1 is home with new support.
whyNot.3: Pathway 3 is a new care home placement for likely long-term needs.

explain.body: Short-term care, rehabilitation and reablement first; long-term needs assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, at home or in a step-down bed.

test.q: Under discharge to assess, when are a person's longer-term care needs assessed?
options: On the day of admission
Before they leave the hospital ward
At their 12-month review
Once they reach optimal recovery
test.why: D2A provides short-term care and rehabilitation, then assesses longer-term needs once the person has reached a point of optimal recovery (Hospital discharge guidance, 2024).

whyNot.0: Needs are not fully known on admission, before recovery.
whyNot.1: Assessing in hospital underestimates potential and delays discharge.
whyNot.2: Waiting a year leaves the person without the right long-term support.

explain.body: NHS trusts must involve patients and unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning (Care Act s74). Local authorities must assess carers who appear to need support (s10).

test.q: A 15-year-old will help care for his mother after discharge. Which duty applies to the NHS trust?
options: To exclude him because he is under 16
To involve him in discharge planning
To ask his school's permission first
To assess his eligibility for any carer's benefits
test.why: Care Act s74 (as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022) requires NHS trusts to involve patients and unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning where appropriate.

whyNot.0: Young carers are specifically included in the duty.
whyNot.3: Benefits assessment is not the trust's discharge duty.

explain.body: Give the person information about diagnoses and treatment and a complete medicines list on transfer; summary to the GP within 24 hours and a copy to the person on the day (NG27).

test.q: Which information does NICE NG27 say people should be given when they transfer between hospital and home?
options: Their consultant's direct contact mobile phone number
A copy of all of their test results since admission
Their full hospital medical record
Their diagnoses, treatment and a full medicines list
test.why: NG27 rec 1.1.5: give people information about their diagnoses and treatment and a complete list of their medicines when they transfer, and to family and carers if appropriate.

whyNot.0: A consultant's personal number is not part of transfer information.
whyNot.1: All test results are not required; the key information is.
whyNot.2: The full record is not routinely given; a clear summary and medicines list are.
